1.1. Raw materials 
Lithium (Li) metal foils were purchased from China Energy Lithium Co., Ltd. 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME, DoDoChem), 1,3-
dioxolane (DOL, DoDoChem), 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropylether (HFE, TCI), LiNO3 (Aladdin), lithium bis-
(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI, DoDoChem), Li2S (Alfa), elemental sulfur (S8, Alfa), aluminum (Al) foils, polypropylene (PP)

1.8. Density functional theory (DFT) calculation 
The DFT calculations were carried out in Gaussian (G16) program[1] with Becke’s three-parameter hybrid method using the Lee–
Yang–Parr correlation functional (B3LYP)[2] at 6-311+G(d,p) level. The solvation effect was considered with the universal solvation 
model of SMD[3] employing parameters of DME. 
The binding energy (Eb) between a lithium polysulfide (LiPS, Li2S8 or Li2S4) and solvents (DME and/or HFE) was defined as 
follows: 
Eb = Ecluster – (ELiPS + Esolvents) 
where Ecluster and ELiPS represent the total energy of the cluster and LiPS, respectively. Esolvents is the total energy of two DME solvents, 
one DME solvent and one HFE solvent, or two HFE solvents that coordinate with LiPS.

2. Electrolyte preparation
The solvent mixtures of DOL/DME (1:1 v/v), DOL/F4DEE (4:1 v/v) and DOL/TTE (4:1 v/v) 
were prepared in advance. Four kinds of electrolyte solutions were then prepared: (1) For Li+ 
solvation study, 1.0 M LiTFSI was dissolved in each single/mixed solvent; (2) For LiPS 
solvation study, Li2S and S8 were mixed with a molar ratio 8:5 and then dissolved in varied 
solvents to reach Li2S6 nominal concentration of 0.1 M; (3) For Li||Carbon paper cell 
construction, 1.0 M LiTFSI and 0.1 M LiNO3 were dissolved in the solutions prepared in (2); 
(4) For Li||S cell construction, 1.0 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiNO3 were dissolved in varied 
solvents. All electrolyte preparation processes were performed in an argon-filled glove-box 
with controlled moisture and oxygen level below 1 ppm.

II. Computational Methods
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed on the Cray cluster Theta of the 
Leadership Computing Facility at Argonne National Laboratory. The simulations were 
carried out in a high-performance mode with version 2.14 of NAMD2, a greatly scalable 
molecular dynamic program used to render an atom-by-atom representation of biomolecules, 
created at the University of Illinois. All electrolyte simulations adopted GAMMP force field3 
generated through GAAMP server on Laboratory Computing Resource Center at Argonne 
National Laboratory. The molar ratios of each molecular species in DOL-DME, DOL-F4DEE 
and DOL-TTE electrolyte with and without the existence of 0.1 M Li2S6 are listed in Table 
S1. The number of atoms for the simulated systems range between 81,830 and 100,000, and 
the dimension of each simulation cell is ~150Å×150Å×150Å. All simulations adopt Periodic 
Boundary Condition under constant NVT condition. The equations of motion were integrated 
with a 2-fs time step, using Langevin dynamics at a temperature of 300 K. To overcome the 
slow dynamics due to the high viscosity of the simulated systems, Hamiltonian simulated 
annealing method (HSA)4 was employed to accelerate the equilibration of MD trajectories. In 
each HSA simulation, 64 independent trajectories were generated, and all of them were used 
to get the statistical average of structural properties. Each trajectory lasts 20 ns, and the last

evidence.excerpt:
1.2. Preparation of electrolytes 
A mixture of DOL/DME (1:1, by vol.) or mixed with 10%, 20% or 30% HFE by volume was first prepared. 1.0 M LiTFSI was then 
dissolved in the above four mixed solvents with 2 wt.% LiNO3 to obtain electrolytes with different solvating power. To prepare the 
electrolyte with Li2S8 or Li2S6, Li2S and S8 were mixed with a molar ratio of 8:7 or 8:5, respectively, in the above electrolytes with a 
concentration of 1.0 M[S]. All the electrolytes were prepared in an argon-filled glove box with O2 and H2O contents below 0.1 ppm.

1.9. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation 
MD simulations were conducted by the Large Scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS) code.[4] Four 
models were constructed to simulate electrolytes without or with 10%, 20%, or 30% HFE by volume for Li2S8 or Li2S4 systems, 
respectively, and the detailed compositions of these models are listed in Tables S6. The force field parameters for solvents were 
generated by the LigParGen web server[5] except that restrained electrostatic potential (RESP) atomic partial charges were assigned 
to each atom, which was obtained based on electrostatic potential (ESP) charges using the Multiwfn program.[6] The parameters for 
Li+, TFSI−, S82−, and S42− were obtained from Jensen et al.,[7] Koddermann et al.,[8] and Rajput et al.,[9] respectively. 
The initial atomic coordinates were generated with Packing Optimization for Molecular Dynamics Simulations (Packmol) 
program.[10] Each system was first equilibrated in the NPT ensemble using the Parrinello–Rahman barostat for 2 ns to maintain a 
temperature of 298 K and a pressure of 1 atm with time constants of 0.1 and 1 ps, respectively.[11] After that, the electrolytes were 
heated from 298 K to 420 K within 2 ns, and maintained at 420 K for 4 ns, followed by annealing from 420 K to 298 K within 2 ns. 
Subsequently, all systems were equilibrated at 298 K in the NPT ensemble for another 4 ns. A 12 ns production run was finally 
conducted in the NVT ensemble under Nose–Hoover thermostat.[12] Only the final 5 ns trajectory was sampled for the analysis of 
solvation structures. The solvation structures were visualized by VESTA.[13]

evidence.excerpt:
1.5 Computational Details
To simulate CE and CPE electrolyte systems over 17,000 atoms, we employed machine learning potentials for molecular dynamics (MLMD) simulations. The initial configurations of Li2S4, LiTFSI, DME, THF and DTL were optimized using Gaussian09 program with M062X/6-311+G(d,p). The CE and CPE electrolyte systems were prepared by randomly placing the molecules in the simulation box based on their experimental densities and molar ratios. For CE electrolyte (0DTL electrolyte), 120 LiTFSI, 74 THF, 738 DME and 30 Li2S4 molecules were added to the simulation box (60*60*60 Å3). For CPE electrolyte (60DTL electrolyte), 120 LiTFSI, 74 THF, 272 DME, 596 DTL and 30 Li2S4 molecules were added to the simulation box (60*60*60 Å3). 

The density functional theory (DFT) dataset was generated through an iterative workflow, which can be outlined as follows:
(1) Initial MD Sampling: We initiated the process by performing MLMD simulations on simplified structures comprising approximately 300 atoms. Each MLMD simulation was conducted for 20 ps with a time step of 0.5 fs.
(2) Model Training: Two independent models, differing only in their initial random seeds, were trained concurrently to assess the robustness of the predictions.
(3) Error Evaluation: After each MLMD simulation, the forces on the sampled structures were predicted using both models. Structures with prediction errors exceeding 0.2 eV/Å between the two models were identified as poorly represented by the potential model and added to a temporary dataset for further processing.
(4) Dataset Augmentation: The temporary dataset was analyzed using SOAP[1] descriptors and K-means[2] clustering to extract up to 300 structurally distinct configurations. These configurations were subjected to DFT calculations, and the resulting data were incorporated into the training dataset to enhance model accuracy.
(5) Iteration: The updated models were then used to perform another round of MLMD simulations.
Steps (3) and (4) were repeated iteratively—MLMD simulation, error evaluation, and dataset augmentation—until the prediction errors of both models were sufficiently minimized.
For the simulations, we employed the M3GNet model[3] with radial and three-body interaction cutoffs set to 5 Å and 4 Å, respectively. The loss function was formulated as a weighted sum of mean squared errors for energies, forces, and stresses, each assigned an equal weight of 1. A batch size of 4 was utilized, along with an exponential learning rate scheduler initialized at 110-3. The convergence criteria for training were set stringently, requiring forces to fall below 0.1 eV/Å. Training was performed on a Tesla A100 GPU until validation errors converged.
After training the potential function model, we performed molecular dynamics simulations on CE and CPE electrolyte systems comprising over 17,000 atoms. The simulations were carried out under NVT ensemble conditions, with the temperature maintained at 300 K, a time step of 0.5 fs, and a total simulation time of 30 ps. The initial 10 ps were designated as the pre-equilibration phase.
In addition, ESPs of molecules were calculated with Gaussian09 program at the B3LYP/def2tzvp level and visualized by GaussView.
